title: equals() / hashCode() Contract
summary: Master the golden rule of Java collections: if a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() MUST equal b.hashCode().
learningObjectives: State the official 3-part contract between equals() and hashCode() in java.lang.Object
Demonstrate how breaking the contract causes HashSet and HashMap to 'lose' objects
Identify the asymmetric converse: equal hash codes do NOT require equal objects (collisions)
Enforce invariant consistency when modifying or extending classes
expectedOutcomes: You can explain the catastrophic collection failures that occur when equals is overridden without hashCode
You will never ship code that violates the equals/hashCode contract

activities.title: Practical Context: The Mandatory Symbiosis of Equality and Hashing

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: You go to a theatre coat check. When you hand the attendant your blue wool coat, they calculate a ticket number (hashCode) based on your seat number and hang your coat in Locker 42. Later, when you return to claim your coat, a different attendant calculates your ticket number using your coat's color instead, assigning ticket number 88. The attendant walks over to Locker 88, opens it, and says: 'Sorry, your coat isn't here! It has vanished!'
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: Your coat was in Locker 42 the entire time. But because the hashing algorithm was inconsistent with identity/equals, the system looked in the wrong bucket. In Java, if two equal objects produce different hash codes, `HashSet.contains()` walks to the wrong bucket and claims the object does not exist!
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: If two objects are equal according to equals(), they MUST produce the exact same hashCode().

activities.content:
One of the most dangerous bugs in enterprise Java is overriding `equals()` without overriding `hashCode()`.

When an object is stored in a `HashSet` or used as a key in a `HashMap`, the collection first queries `hashCode()` to find the bucket before invoking `equals()`.

Violating this contract causes objects to vanish inside collections, leading to catastrophic data loss.

activities.title: The equals() and hashCode() Contract: The Golden Rule of Java Collections
Catastrophic Failure: The Ghost Object in HashSet
activities.explanation: Because hashCode() was omitted, item1 and item2 produce different memory-based hashes. HashSet looks in the wrong bucket and returns false.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `item2` has a different default hash code from `item1`.
`warehouse.contains(item2)` computes `item2.hashCode()`, searches a different bucket, and returns `false`.

activities.title: Contract Restored: Flawless HashSet Lookup
activities.explanation: Overriding both equals() and hashCode() guarantees that matching items calculate the exact same bucket index.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `new FixedItem("SKU-400")` produces the exact same hash code as `searchTarget`.
`warehouse.contains` navigates straight to the correct bucket.
Inside that bucket, `equals()` confirms the match and returns `true`.

questions.question: Which statement correctly represents the golden contract between equals() and hashCode()?
options: If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() MUST be true
If a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(), then a.equals(b) MUST be true
If a.equals(b) is false, then a.hashCode() must not equal b.hashCode()
hashCode() must return positive numbers only
questions.explanation: The contract strictly states that equal objects must have equal hash codes.

questions.question: What happens if a class overrides equals() but fails to override hashCode()?
options: The compiler rejects the class
Instances of the class will fail to work properly in hash-based collections (HashSet, HashMap)
The JVM crashes with a ClassFormatError
Memory leaks occur immediately
questions.explanation: Omitting hashCode causes equal objects to hash to different buckets, making HashSet/HashMap lookups fail.

questions.question: If two objects have the same hashCode(), are they guaranteed to be equal according to equals()?
options: Yes, always
No, two unequal objects may produce the same hash code due to a hash collision
Only if both are strings
Only if the hash code is prime
questions.explanation: Hash collisions mean distinct objects can share the same hash code; they are not required to be equal.

questions.question: What happens when you add an object to a HashSet, mutate one of its fields that is used in hashCode(), and then call set.contains(obj)?
options: It returns true
It returns false because the mutated hash code points to a different bucket
The set automatically updates its buckets
An ConcurrentModificationException is thrown
questions.explanation: Mutating a key after insertion changes its hash code, so subsequent searches look in the wrong bucket and fail.

questions.question: Why are keys in a HashMap or elements in a HashSet strongly recommended to be IMMUTABLE?
options: To prevent changes to equals/hashCode fields that would make the object unretrievable from the collection
Because Java forbids mutable classes in packages
To prevent multithreading
Because final classes run 50% faster
questions.explanation: Immutability guarantees that an object's hash code and equality never change while stored in a hash structure.

questions.question: If a class overrides neither equals() nor hashCode(), does it violate the contract?
options: Yes, all classes must override both
No, default java.lang.Object implementations satisfy the contract based on memory address identity
Only if it is public
Only if it has fields
questions.explanation: Object's default implementations (identity equals and identity hashCode) satisfy the contract perfectly.

questions.question: In a HashMap, what role does hashCode() play vs equals()?
options: hashCode() locates the bucket in O(1); equals() confirms the exact key match within that bucket
equals() finds the bucket; hashCode() confirms the key
They both do the exact same thing
hashCode() is only used for sorting
questions.explanation: hashCode() is the quick bucket locator; equals() is the definitive content comparator.

questions.question: What tool or feature in modern IDEs prevents equals/hashCode contract bugs?
options: Code Generation wizards that generate both equals() and hashCode() simultaneously from selected fields
A special compiler plugin called AntiBug
Garbage collection logs
Auto-formatting code
questions.explanation: IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse, VS Code) provide generators that generate paired, consistent equals and hashCode methods.

questions.question: If you override hashCode(), are you required to override equals()?
options: Technically no, but practically yes: changing hashCode without overriding equals leaves equals based on identity, which is almost always a design error
It is illegal in bytecode
Only if the class is abstract
No, never
questions.explanation: Overriding one without the other almost always signals a conceptual bug in domain modeling.

questions.question: What is the consequence of adding an object to a HashSet twice if equals/hashCode are properly implemented?
options: The set contains two copies
The second addition is rejected, keeping size at 1 (no duplicates)
An exception is thrown
The first copy is deleted
questions.explanation: A Set forbids duplicates; properly implemented equals and hashCode allow the set to detect and reject the duplicate.

questions.question: What is the single most common interview question on the equals/hashCode contract?
questions.answer: 'What happens if you override equals() without overriding hashCode()?' The candidate must explain: Equal objects will produce different hash codes (derived from memory address). When added to a HashSet or HashMap, the object will be placed in one bucket, but searching for an identical object will compute a different hash and look in a different bucket, returning false. The object becomes an unfindable ghost.
questions.expectedAnswer: 'What happens if you override equals() without overriding hashCode()?' The candidate must explain: Equal objects will produce different hash codes (derived from memory address). When added to a HashSet or HashMap, the object will be placed in one bucket, but searching for an identical object will compute a different hash and look in a different bucket, returning false. The object becomes an unfindable ghost.
questions.keyTakeaway: Omission of hashCode breaks hash collections: equal objects end up in different buckets.
keyPoints: Omission of hashCode breaks hash collections: equal objects end up in different buckets.

questions.question: Can you explain why the converse statement is false: 'If hashCode is the same, equals must be true'?
questions.answer: A hash code is a 32-bit int with only ~4.3 billion possible values. There are infinite possible distinct strings or objects. By the Pigeonhole Principle, two completely different objects (e.g. "FB" and "Ea") can produce the exact same integer hash code (3136). This is a collision, and `equals()` will correctly return `false`.
questions.expectedAnswer: A hash code is a 32-bit int with only ~4.3 billion possible values. There are infinite possible distinct strings or objects. By the Pigeonhole Principle, two completely different objects (e.g. "FB" and "Ea") can produce the exact same integer hash code (3136). This is a collision, and `equals()` will correctly return `false`.
questions.keyTakeaway: Collisions are mathematically inevitable; equal hashes do not imply equal objects.
keyPoints: Collisions are mathematically inevitable; equal hashes do not imply equal objects.

questions.question: What happens if a mutable field used in hashCode() is changed while the object is a key in a HashMap?
questions.answer: The object's hash code changes, but its position in the internal array table remains at the old bucket index. When `map.get(key)` is called, it recomputes the new hash code, navigates to the new (wrong) bucket, and fails to find the entry. The key-value pair is permanently leaked and cannot even be removed.
questions.expectedAnswer: The object's hash code changes, but its position in the internal array table remains at the old bucket index. When `map.get(key)` is called, it recomputes the new hash code, navigates to the new (wrong) bucket, and fails to find the entry. The key-value pair is permanently leaked and cannot even be removed.
questions.keyTakeaway: Mutating a key after insertion corrupts its bucket placement, causing permanent memory leaks.
keyPoints: Mutating a key after insertion corrupts its bucket placement, causing permanent memory leaks.

questions.question: How do records in Java prevent equals/hashCode contract bugs?
questions.answer: Java records automatically generate paired, canonical implementations of `equals()` and `hashCode()` that inspect the exact same set of component fields. Because records are shallowly immutable, keys cannot be mutated after insertion into hash structures.
questions.expectedAnswer: Java records automatically generate paired, canonical implementations of `equals()` and `hashCode()` that inspect the exact same set of component fields. Because records are shallowly immutable, keys cannot be mutated after insertion into hash structures.
questions.keyTakeaway: Records automate contract compliance and guarantee immutability.
keyPoints: Records automate contract compliance and guarantee immutability.

questions.question: What happens if equals() compares 3 fields, but hashCode() only hashes 2 of them?
questions.answer: This does NOT violate the contract! If all 3 fields are equal, then the 2 hashed fields must also be equal, so `hashCode()` will still return equal results. However, it can increase hash collisions if many objects differ only on that third unhashed field.
questions.expectedAnswer: This does NOT violate the contract! If all 3 fields are equal, then the 2 hashed fields must also be equal, so `hashCode()` will still return equal results. However, it can increase hash collisions if many objects differ only on that third unhashed field.
questions.keyTakeaway: Omitting a field from hashCode does not break the contract, but increases collision rates.
keyPoints: Omitting a field from hashCode does not break the contract, but increases collision rates.

questions.question: What happens if hashCode() hashes 3 fields, but equals() only compares 2 of them?
questions.answer: This IS A FATAL CONTRACT VIOLATION! Two objects could be equal according to `equals()` (because the 2 compared fields match), but produce DIFFERENT hash codes (because the third uncompared field differed). This will break hash tables!
questions.expectedAnswer: This IS A FATAL CONTRACT VIOLATION! Two objects could be equal according to `equals()` (because the 2 compared fields match), but produce DIFFERENT hash codes (because the third uncompared field differed). This will break hash tables!
questions.keyTakeaway: Never include a field in hashCode that is ignored by equals().
keyPoints: Never include a field in hashCode that is ignored by equals().

practiceProblems.title: Fixing the Broken HashSet Item Lookup
practiceProblems.problemStatement: The `InventoryBadge` class below overrides `equals` but forgot `hashCode`, so `badgeSet.contains(target)` returns `false`! Fix `InventoryBadge` by adding the `@Override public int hashCode()` method using `java.util.Objects.hash(badgeCode)` so the set successfully finds the item.
hints: Add `@Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(badgeCode); }`.
Once hashCode matches, badgeSet finds the badge.

practiceProblems.title: Pair of Objects Contract Validator
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build an automated contract compliance tester from scratch:
1. Class `ContractValidator`: method `public static boolean verifyContract(Object a, Object b)`:
   - Evaluates `boolean eq = a.equals(b);`.
   - Evaluates `boolean hashEq = (a.hashCode() == b.hashCode());`.
   - If `eq` is true and `hashEq` is false: prints `'VIOLATION: Objects are equal, but hashCodes differ!'` and returns false.
   - Otherwise, prints `'COMPLIANT: Contract satisfied'` and returns true.
2. In `Main`, create class `GoodEntity(int id)` with paired equals and hashCode. Create `BadEntity(int id)` with equals only.
3. Test `verifyContract` on two GoodEntity(10) instances (prints COMPLIANT).
4. Test `verifyContract` on two BadEntity(10) instances (prints VIOLATION).
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
COMPLIANT: Contract satisfied
VIOLATION: Objects are equal, but hashCodes differ!
hints: Check `if (eq && !hashEq)` to detect the golden rule violation.

practiceProblems.title: Eliminating Duplicate Registrations with HashSet
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a unique member registry that prevents duplicate registrations using `HashSet` from scratch:
1. Class `VipMember`: holds `private String nationalId` and `private String fullName`.
   - Constructor initializes both.
   - Implement paired `equals` and `hashCode` based SOLELY on `nationalId` (since nationalId is the unique identifier).
2. Class `MemberRegistry`: holds `private java.util.Set<VipMember> members = new java.util.HashSet<>()`.
   - Method `public boolean register(VipMember m)`: returns `members.add(m)`.
   - Method `public int totalCount()`: returns `members.size()`.
3. In `Main`, register VipMember('NID-100', 'Alice Cooper') (returns true). Register VipMember('NID-100', 'Alice C.') (returns false because national ID is duplicate!). Register VipMember('NID-200', 'Bob Dylan') (returns true). Print total count (2).
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Registered Alice: true
Registered Dup:   false
Registered Bob:   true
Total count:      2
hints: HashSet.add() returns false when an equal element (matching equals and hashCode) already exists in the set.

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Contract Violation Caused by Field Mismatch
practiceProblems.problemStatement: In the code below, `equals()` checks `firstName` AND `lastName`, but `hashCode()` hashes `firstName` ONLY. As a result, two people with the same first name but different last names share the same hash, but even worse, if a developer refactors to only compare `firstName`, the code behaves unpredictably. Fix `PersonKey` so that `equals()` and `hashCode()` use the EXACT same fields: `firstName` AND `lastName`.

practiceProblems.title: Mutable Key Corruption Post-Mortem Simulator
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a simulation demonstrating the danger of mutating a key stored in a HashMap from scratch:
1. Class `MutableAccount`: holds `private String accountId`. Constructor initializes it. Method `public void setAccountId(String newId)` mutates accountId.
   - Override `equals(Object o)` comparing accountId.
   - Override `hashCode()` returning `Objects.hash(accountId)`.
2. In `Main`:
   - Create `java.util.HashMap<MutableAccount, String> accountMap = new HashMap<>()`.
   - Create account = new MutableAccount("ORIGINAL-ID");
   - Put account into map with value "Active Account Profile".
   - Verify `accountMap.containsKey(account)` is true.
   - Now MUTATE the key: `account.setAccountId("MUTATED-ID");`
   - Check `accountMap.containsKey(account)`: print `'Contains mutated key: ' + accountMap.containsKey(account)` (prints false!).
   - Print `'Map size: ' + accountMap.size()` (prints 1, proving the entry is trapped in the wrong bucket!).
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Contains mutated key: false
Map size: 1
hints: Mutating accountId changes the hash code returned by acc.hashCode().
containsKey searches the bucket for MUTATED-ID, but the entry sits in the bucket for ORIGINAL-ID!
